title: A meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students
extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether technology-delivered literacy instruction improves literacy outcomes for elementary students and what study, participant, instructional, or outcome characteristics might moderate those effects. The authors note that prior reviews often focused on narrow literacy domains, restricted student populations, or specific technologies, and many did not use meta-analytic methods to estimate overall effects and moderators.

The intervention studied was technology-delivered literacy instruction provided through devices such as computers, tablets, or smartphones. Across the included studies, programs targeted a range of literacy skills including phonological awareness, phonics/decoding/word reading, spelling, vocabulary, fluency, comprehension, and writing. The meta-analysis included 53 experimental or quasi-experimental studies published between 2000 and 2022, analyzing norm- or criterion-referenced literacy outcomes only.

The population was elementary-aged students, primarily Grades K-5, with most studies concentrated in Grades K-2. About half the studies involved students with or at risk for reading difficulties. Nearly all interventions were delivered in school settings, mostly via computers or laptops, and most programs were multicomponent and publicly available. The average intervention duration was 18 weeks, with about 36 minutes per day, 4 days per week, averaging 37 total instructional hours.

The main conclusion is that technology-delivered literacy instruction had a small but statistically significant positive effect on literacy outcomes (g = 0.24, p < .001). Moderator analyses found no statistically significant differences by publication type, research design, sample size, grade band, reading difficulty status, dosage, public availability, instructional content, or outcome domain. The authors conclude that elementary students are likely to benefit from technology-delivered literacy instruction, but more research is needed to determine what works best for whom and under what conditions.

identified_tools.name: Technology-delivered literacy instruction — pooled
identified_tools.description: Pooled category covering technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary learners, including computer-, tablet-, and other device-based instruction targeting literacy skills such as phonological awareness, decoding/word reading, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, spelling, and writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Meta-analysis of technology-delivered literacy instruction for elementary students in Grades K-5 (with some included samples spanning pre-K to grade 8 if the majority were in K-5). The review included 53 experimental or quasi-experimental studies of literacy instruction delivered via technological devices in English, compared against groups not receiving technology-delivered literacy instruction.

findings.finding_summary: Across 53 experimental or quasi-experimental studies, technology-delivered literacy instruction had a statistically significant positive overall effect on norm- or criterion-referenced literacy outcomes for elementary students. The reported mean effect was g=0.24 (p<.001), indicating a small benefit relative to comparison conditions not receiving technology-delivered literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: ABRACADABRA
identified_tools.description: A publicly available technology-delivered literacy instruction program; expanded in the review as 'A Balanced Approach for Children Designed to Achieve Best Results for All.'
identified_tools.use_case: The review identifies ABRACADABRA as the most frequently studied named program among included treatment conditions. It was used in 12 treatment conditions/studies, including Abrami et al. (2016), Guo (2018), Lysenko and Abrami (2014), Lysenko et al. (2019; both treatment groups), Mak et al. (2017), Piquette et al. (2014), Savage et al. (2009; both synthetic and analytic phonics versions), Savage et al. (2013), Sha and Savage (2020), and Wolgemuth et al. (2013). The review codes it as addressing multiple literacy domains across studies, including combinations of phonological awareness, word reading/decoding, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and writing. It is discussed as a publicly available literacy program contributing to the overall positive meta-analytic effect of technology-delivered literacy instruction.

identified_tools.name: Read Naturally
identified_tools.description: A publicly available literacy intervention program focused on reading practice and development.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Arvans (2009). In this review it is coded as addressing vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is one of the named publicly available literacy programs contributing to the review's pool of technology-delivered instruction studies.

identified_tools.name: The First 4,000 Words
identified_tools.description: A publicly available literacy program used for technology-delivered instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Beaudry (2014). The review codes it as targeting vocabulary and text reading/fluency. It is mentioned as one of the specific named interventions evaluated in the meta-analysis.

identified_tools.name: Fast ForWord
identified_tools.description: A publicly available computer-based literacy intervention program used to support reading-related skill development.
identified_tools.use_case: The review notes that Fast ForWord was used in five treatment conditions. It appears in Boller (2010), Loeb et al. (2009; one treatment arm), Reed (2013), Soboleski (2011), and Troia (2004). Across studies, it was coded as targeting combinations of phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and related reading skills. The review highlights it as one of the most commonly used named programs in the included corpus.

identified_tools.name: Alphie's Alley
identified_tools.description: A publicly available literacy instruction program delivered through technology.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Chambers et al. (2008). The review codes it as addressing phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is mentioned as one of the specific products evaluated in the meta-analysis.

identified_tools.name: Reading Upgrade
identified_tools.description: A publicly available technology-based reading instruction program.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Cole and Hilliard (2006). The review codes it as targeting phonological awareness, word reading, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is part of the review's set of named literacy interventions.

identified_tools.name: Vocabulators
identified_tools.description: A literacy intervention system focused on vocabulary-related instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in Fogarty et al. (2020). The review marks it as not publicly available and codes it as addressing vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is one of the named interventions studied in the review.

identified_tools.name: Spelling FLASH
identified_tools.description: A technology-delivered spelling instruction program.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the intervention in Fuchs et al. (2006). The review codes it specifically as targeting encoding/spelling. It is a named tool in the meta-analysis corpus but no separate tool-specific synthesis is reported.

identified_tools.name: Waterford Early Reading Program
identified_tools.description: A publicly available early reading instruction program delivered via technology.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in Hecht and Close (2002) and in both treatment groups of Shamir and Johnson (2012). The review codes it as addressing phonological awareness and word reading in one study, and broader combinations including vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension in others. It is one of the named publicly available literacy programs represented in the meta-analysis.

identified_tools.name: Comprehension Booster
identified_tools.description: A publicly available technology-based literacy program focused on comprehension-related instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Horne (2017). The review codes it as targeting vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is named as one of the interventions reviewed.

identified_tools.name: READ 180
identified_tools.description: A publicly available blended/technology-supported literacy intervention program for reading development.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in Kim et al. (2010) and Kim et al. (2011). The review codes it as addressing word reading, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is one of the named, publicly available multicomponent literacy programs in the included studies.

identified_tools.use_case: Included as Treatment 1 in Knezek and Christensen (2007). The review marks it as not publicly available and codes it as spanning phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and writing. It is discussed only as a named intervention condition in the included studies.

identified_tools.name: CAREER system
identified_tools.description: A named literacy instruction system delivered through technology.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Lan et al. (2009). The review codes it as addressing word reading, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. It is one of the specifically named non-publicly available systems in the included studies.

identified_tools.description: A publicly available literacy program for early reading-related skills.
identified_tools.use_case: Appears in Loeb et al. (2009) as part of a treatment arm combining Earobics and Laureate Learning. The review codes that treatment arm as addressing phonological awareness and comprehension. Earobics is explicitly named in the review as a component of an included intervention condition.

identified_tools.name: Laureate Learning
identified_tools.description: A publicly available educational software product line used here for literacy instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: Appears in Loeb et al. (2009) as part of a treatment arm combining Earobics and Laureate Learning. The review codes that intervention as targeting phonological awareness and comprehension. It is mentioned as part of a named combined treatment condition.

identified_tools.name: Imagine Learning English
identified_tools.description: A publicly available technology-based English/literacy learning program.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as the treatment in Longberg (2012). The review codes it as covering phonological awareness, word reading, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and writing. It is a named multicomponent literacy intervention in the included corpus.

identified_tools.name: ePearl
identified_tools.description: A named digital literacy/learning support system used alongside other literacy software.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in Lysenko and Abrami (2014) in combination with ABRACADABRA. The review lists the treatment as 'ABRACADABRA and ePearl' and codes it as addressing phonological awareness, word reading, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and writing. ePearl is therefore explicitly discussed as part of a named intervention package.

identified_tools.name: READS
identified_tools.description: A named literacy instruction/support system used in conjunction with ABRACADABRA.
identified_tools.use_case: Included in Lysenko et al. (2019) in two treatment conditions listed as 'ABRACADABRA and READS.' The review codes these treatment arms as addressing word reading, spelling, text reading/fluency, comprehension, and writing. READS is explicitly named as part of these intervention conditions.

identified_tools.name: Lexia
identified_tools.description: A publicly available literacy software system for reading instruction.
identified_tools.use_case: The review states that seven treatment conditions used Lexia Learning Systems, and Table 4 specifically lists Lexia in Macaruso et al. (2006), Macaruso and Walker (2008), Macaruso and Rodman (2011), O'Callaghan et al. (2016), Schechter et al. (2015), Stein et al. (2022; one treatment arm), and Whittaker (2013). Across studies it was coded as addressing combinations of phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. The review treats Lexia as one of the most commonly studied named literacy programs.

identified_tools.name: Daisy Quest
identified_tools.description: A publicly available early literacy software program.
identified_tools.use_case: Appears in Mathes et al. (2001) and Mitchell and Fox (2001) as part of the combined intervention 'Daisy Quest and Daisy's Castle.' The review codes these interventions as targeting phonological awareness. Daisy Quest is explicitly named as part of included treatment conditions.

identified_tools.use_case: Appears in Mathes et al. (2001) and Mitchell and Fox (2001) alongside Daisy Quest. The review codes the combined intervention as addressing phonological awareness. It is specifically named in the review as part of included literacy software interventions.

The review codes it as addressing phonological awareness, word reading, spelling, vocabulary, text reading/fluency, and comprehension. quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of 53 experimental and quasi-experimental studies, which places it in the highest evidence category. However, the included studies were heterogeneous and some reporting gaps remain.
impact_tier_rationale: The meta-analysis found a statistically significant positive overall effect on literacy outcomes (g = 0.24), which meets the threshold for blue impact. The effect applies to an important K-12 population: elementary students, including many with or at risk for reading difficulties.
